failures.title: Audi CRLB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: AdBlue System and NOx Sensor Failures - 2012-2020 models
items.whatHappens: The EA288 relies heavily on AdBlue injection for Euro 6 compliance. Heater elements within the AdBlue tank and the downstream NOx sensors are prone to failure. This triggers an "Emissions Malfunction" warning on the dashboard and frequently forces the vehicle into limp mode, restricting power and preventing engine restarts after a certain mileage countdown.
items.repairVsReplace: If the engine block and internals are healthy, replacing the AdBlue tank/sensor assembly (£400-£1,500) is the correct fix. However, if chronic AdBlue crystallisation has caused secondary overheating or EGR cooler leaks, a full Audi CRLB engine replacement becomes the more reliable long-term solution. Read our full AdBlue system failure guide.

items.title: DPF Clogging (Urban Use) - All CRLB variants
items.whatHappens: Frequent short trips prevent the Diesel Particulate Filter from reaching the high temperatures required for active regeneration. Soot builds up, increasing exhaust backpressure. Over time, this restricts airflow, leading to turbocharger strain, reduced performance, and potential oil dilution as unburnt fuel washes past the piston rings.
items.repairVsReplace: A professional DPF clean or forced regeneration can resolve early-stage clogging. If the DPF is physically cracked or the turbo has suffered oil starvation due to blocked return lines, a reconditioned CRLB engine is often more cost-effective than piecemeal component replacement. Read our full DPF clogging guide.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CRLB (EA288) is generally considered significantly more robust than its predecessor, the EA189, with timing chain issues being far less prevalent. Post-2015 software updates also improved AdBlue dosing reliability, making later-model CRLB units a safer bet .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CRLB
variants.intro: The Audi CRLB engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and the transmission bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from your 17-digit VIN.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Audi CRLB - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Audi CRLB engine is a viable option only if it comes with a verifiable service history proving regular oil changes and a recent DPF/AdBlue system health check. Without this documentation, you risk inheriting hidden carbon buildup or failing NOx sensors that will trigger limp mode shortly after installation. Explore vetted options via our used engines network.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned CRLB is the recommended choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will include a refreshed turbocharger, new EGR and AdBlue components, and a cleaned or replaced DPF, directly addressing the EA288's known weak points and restoring the engine to near-factory reliability. Compare reconditioned engines today.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage CRLB units that have suffered secondary damage, such as turbo failure leading to oil starvation or severe AdBlue crystallisation damaging the block. An upgraded rebuild should include revised piston rings and an updated water pump assembly to prevent future coolant leaks. Learn more about rebuilt engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Opting for a supply-and-fit service through our network ensures the replacement is performed by Audi specialists, with the warranty backed by the installing garage for complete peace of mind. View our supply and fit options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CRLB is typically found in Audi A3 (8V), A4 (B9), and Q5 (8R/FY) models valued between £5,000 and £22,000 . For lower-value examples (sub-£5,000), a reconditioned engine costing £2,800+ may approach or exceed 60% of the vehicle's current market value. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the CRLB engine?
items.answer: The most frequent documented issue with the Audi CRLB is AdBlue system failure, specifically NOx sensor or heater malfunctions. This triggers an "Emissions Malfunction" warning and can force the vehicle into limp mode. DPF clogging from frequent short urban trips is the second most common failure pattern.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CRLB engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Audi CRLB is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known risks of inherited AdBlue and DPF issues. Used engines carry a 3-6 month warranty and may have undocumented urban wear. Reconditioned units include refreshed emission components and a 12-24 month warranty.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the CRLB engine?
items.answer: The CRLB engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, near the transmission bell housing, and is listed on your V5C registration document. It is commonly confused with earlier EA189 codes like CRBC or later CNHA variants. Fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU mapping and turbo plumbing mismatches.
